headlines.summary: Equinix says smaller data centers may be less exposed to U.S. restrictions as scrutiny of AI infrastructure grows.
headlines.article_text: Equinix bets on smaller data centers amid growing U.S. scrutiny Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Equinix's enterprise data centers are typically smaller than the projects drawing U.S. regulatory scrutiny, according to Cyrus Adaggra, the firm's Asia-Pacific president. The company's capital spending has risen to $7 billion, while third-quarter annualized gross bookings jumped 35% from a year earlier. Slower U.S. data center construction could weigh on Asian chip suppliers, while some investment may shift to Asia, according to reports. In this article EQIX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Inside one of Equinix's internal operations at Equinix Data Center in Ashburn, Virginia, on May 9, 2024. Amanda Andrade-Rhoades | The Washington Post | Getty Images Equinix says its smaller data centers could be less exposed to potential U.S. construction restrictions as regulators scrutinize the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. The company's facilities typically range from 30 to 60 megawatts, compared with the roughly 100-megawatt threshold that Cyrus Adaggra, Equinix's Asia-Pacific president, said is generally targeted by U.S. proposals. "We will invest in markets where we see customer demand, and because we have a footprint that is typically less than 100 megawatts, we tend not to fall and be caught by the legislation or the regulation, which is typically at about 100 megawatts in the U.S.," Adaggra told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia. " watch now VIDEO 4:02 04:02 Equinix data center demand with $7 Billion capex push amid AI Jitters Squawk Box Asia His comments come as the U.S. midterm election results have heightened concerns that new restrictions on data center development could delay projects and raise construction costs. About 53% of projected growth in the U.S. hyperscaler development pipeline is concentrated in states where newly elected governors could impose restrictions on data center construction, according to a Wednesday report from BMI, a Fitch Solutions company. The firm said any impact would likely become more apparent from 2028, as most projects planned for 2027 are already committed. Demand fuels expansion Equinix has increased capital spending from about $2 billion a few years ago to $7 billion, driven by growing customer demand, Adaggra said. "The number one determinant of our capex spend and build is customer demand," he said. Annualized gross bookings exceeded $500 million for the first time in the third quarter, up 35% from a year earlier. Adaggra said growth was driven by demand from large enterprises, including Fortune 500 companies, as businesses invest in hybrid and multi-cloud infrastructure, network connectivity and access to digital infrastructure. Equinix serves about 60% of Fortune 500 companies, he added. Potential restrictions on data center development could also raise costs across the AI infrastructure supply chain, according to Russell Investments. The investment firm also flagged that slower U.S. data center construction could weigh on demand for semiconductors and other infrastructure equipment, including from suppliers across Asia. Asia gains momentum Asia is also emerging as a major destination for data center investment. "After the U.S., we expect actually most data center investments and activity to happen in Asia," Sjoerd Leenart, CEO of JPMorgan 's banking business in Asia Pacific, said in a podcast released Friday. Global hyperscalers are seeking Asian markets with sufficient land, electricity and grid capacity, Leenart said. Some of that investment could be spread across several markets, according to a Thursday report from Mirae Asset Securities. The brokerage said South Korea could emerge as a key market for additional capacity in Asia, with operators that secure power, land and long-term customer contracts better positioned to expand. However, Asia faces its own constraints. Power availability, grid connectivity and equipment delays remain as key challenges for data center development, according to a Thursday report from risk advisory and insurance brokerage WTW. Leenart also pointed to regulatory pushback in Thailand and Australia, where he said authorities had paused some projects to assess the impact of data center energy demand on other industries and consumers. headlines.summary: Bob McNally predicts that both Brent and West Texas Intermediate futures will jump above $100.
headlines.article_text: Rapidan Energy sees oil spike as U.S.-Iran military action risk rises Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Bob McNally, CEO of geopolitical and energy analysis firm Rapidan Energy Group said he foresees a 80% chance that the world will see "a resumption of military fighting." He predicts that both Brent and West Texas Intermediate futures will jump above $100. Iranian speaker of parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has taken aim at U.S. Vice President JD Vance, calling his reaction to the Republican loss in the midterms a "losing gambler energy." A flight deck director signals an F-35C Lightning II on the flight deck aboard the USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) during Exercise RIMPAC (Rim of the Pacific) 2026 while underway in the Pacific Ocean near Hawaii on July 17, 2026. Michelle Bir | Afp | Getty Images The U.S. is likely to resume military action against Iran in the coming days, a move that could send oil prices sharply higher, according to Bob McNally, CEO of geopolitical and energy analysis firm Rapidan Energy Group. Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," McNally put the odds of "a resumption of military fighting" at 80% as the U.S. midterm elections recede. McNally said he expects both Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude futures to rise above $100 a barrel. The benchmarks are currently trading at about $100 and $91, respectively. watch now VIDEO 4:50 04:50 80% odds of renewed military attack in Iran, oil risk premium to head higher Squawk Box Asia Oil prices had spiked above the $100 mark ahead of the midterm elections as investors weighed uncertainty surrounding the Iran conflict and the risk of further U.S. military actions. President Donald Trump had previously said he would not launch new attacks on Iran before the elections, though The Wall Street Journal revealed that Washington had carried out limited strikes, according to U.S. officials. "President Donald Trump is determined, as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally said. "The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it. And as long as that core difference in that deal space is absent, the escalation dynamic remains in place," he added. McNally's view is shared by other analysts, including Lombard Odier's chief economist Samy Chaar and head of investment strategy Luca Bindelli. In a Nov.4 note , they said the "lame duck" period before the new Congress is sworn in could give Trump a window to resume strikes against Iran. Any renewed campaign, however, could be constrained in duration and effectiveness by pressure on U.S. munitions supplies. Other analysts see the midterm results as creating more room for diplomacy. Norbert Rücker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer said the market had become "more convinced" that the end of the midterms could provide a diplomatic off-ramp rather than lead to renewed escalation. That possibility increased with Iran reportedly sending the U.S. a nuclear proposal through Qatar, Reuters reported Friday, citing a senior Iranian official . But the proposal would be discussed only after Washington meets what Tehran described as "seven demands," ‌including an end to U.S. "acts of aggression," the naval blockade of Iranian ports and what it called economic warfare, as well as the release of Iranian assets. In return, Iran will allow ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz. The official also told Reuters that Washington was reviewing the proposal but ​declined to provide further details. Political fallout grows Separately, Iran's speaker of parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf took aim at U.S. Vice President JD Vance after Vance blamed the war with Iran for Republicans' midterm losses. In a post on X , Ghalibaf described Vance's reaction as "losing gambler energy" and said that Vance "can't walk away from the table." He also accused the Trump administration of preparing the next phase of conflict. "Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?" Ghalibaf wrote, in an apparent reference to Trump. Iranian Parliament Speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, gestures while speaking with media in a media conference at a conference hall in the Iranian Parliament building in Tehran, Iran, on Dec. 2, 2025. Morteza Nikoubazl | Nurphoto | Getty Images Vance posted on Nov. 4 that "the reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," adding that a pollster he consulted found that ending the war was the top issue cited by former Trump voters who had switched to Democrats. Cost of living and inflation were also among these concerns. Vance has at times pushed for diplomacy with Tehran. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that he had reached out to an Iranian hard-liner in an effort to revive peace talks. The war has also contributed to higher global energy costs, which have fed into broader concerns over inflation and the cost of living.
